title: The Weighted Thread: Brittnau, the Roman Quarry, and the Drawings Addressed to the Next Century
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brittnau: the weaver's daughter, tenth of ten
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date given identically by English and German Wikipedia and by the Emma Kunz Zentrum
stops.campa: In the Wiggertal, in a house that lives on a hand weaver's wages, Rosina Kunz bears a daughter on the twenty-third of May and the family names her Emma. She is one of ten children, and three of them will not survive infancy. Brittnau is a village of looms and small farms, and nothing about the house is remarkable. Her father Stephan Oswald Kunz works thread into cloth by hand, one of the last in the valley who can still make a living that way. The daughter will spend her working life holding a weighted thread over paper, and she will keep coming back to this valley to do it.
suggested_refs: The weaving village of Brittnau in the Wiggertal, Aargau

stops.name: Brittnau: the child who answers questions no one asked
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the childhood sensitivity is reported only in family-derived biography relayed by English and German Wikipedia, with no year attached. The date is a placement inside her school years, not an attested event
stops.campa: She attends the village primary school and does well enough that nobody writes it down. What the household notices instead is a strangeness: the child answers questions no one asked aloud and names trouble before it announces itself. In a poor village such a thing is not called a gift, it is called odd, and odd is kept quiet. She keeps it quiet for twenty years. Every account of these years reaches the record through the family rather than through a document, and the girl herself leaves nothing written from them.
suggested_refs: The primary school of Brittnau in the 1890s

stops.name: Brittnau: two of the house dead by their own hand
stops.date_confidence: attested to her seventeenth year by German Wikipedia; no source consulted gives a month, a day, or the interval between the two deaths, and none says they fell close together
stops.campa: In her seventeenth year her father dies by his own hand, and a brother dies by his own hand. No account explains either death, and no account states how far apart they fell. The house that has already buried three infants buries two grown men. Emma says almost nothing about it for the rest of her life. What she does say later is procedure rather than grief: that suffering can be located and in some cases turned. No source describes the room those two years were spent in, and no photograph of the household survives from them.
suggested_refs: The Kunz household at Brittnau, 1909

stops.name: Brittnau: the weight on the thread, and a year across the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: the pendulum work at about eighteen is attested by German Wikipedia; the 1911 crossing to the United States is attested by the same source, but its destination, employment, and household are a documentary gap no source consulted fills
stops.campa: At eighteen she takes up a pendulum, a weight on a thread held over paper, and begins testing what her contemporaries call telepathy and prophecy. She names no teacher and claims none afterward; the practice arrives as a fact about herself rather than a skill acquired. The next year she crosses the Atlantic to the United States, reportedly following a man, and returns within about a year, disappointed. No source names the city, the work, or the household that took her in. She is back in the Wiggertal before she is twenty, and she takes up the thread again.
suggested_refs: Swiss emigration records for the 1911 sailing season, unlocated for Kunz

stops.name: Strengelbach: eleven years at the knitting machines
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia gives the knitting factory at Strengelbach and the span 1912 to 1923, without month
stops.campa: A few kilometers from home, at a knitting factory in Strengelbach, she takes work tending machines that turn thread into cloth as her father turned it by hand. She is twenty. The job holds her eleven years, through her twenties and into her thirties, and the record of that decade is the dates and nothing else: no letters, no incident, no notice taken by anyone. She keeps the pendulum work underneath the shift schedule, tested in private and mentioned to almost nobody, until the factory years run out and something else takes her.
suggested_refs: The knitting works at Strengelbach, Aargau, employer 1912-1923

stops.name: Engelberg: the summers in Jakob Welti's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia dates the arrangement 1923 to 1939 and specifies that the Engelberg part of it ran during the summer months only, so this was seasonal employment rather than a continuous sixteen-year residence
stops.campa: She leaves the knitting machines for the household of the painter Jakob Welti, keeping house for him and keeping him company. The arrangement runs sixteen years and takes her to Engelberg only through the summer months; when the season closes she goes back to the Aargau. Engelberg is a mountain village under the Titlis, thin air and visitors, and it puts her for the first time inside a working artist's rooms, near stretched canvas and ground pigment, in a life organised around making images. Welti does not teach her to draw.
suggested_refs: The household of the painter Jakob Welti at Engelberg, Obwalden

stops.name: Engelberg: sixteen seasons in another person's rooms
stops.date_confidence: traditional; a placement inside the attested 1923-1939 arrangement. Welti's attitude to her research is nowhere recorded and the reading offered here is reconstruction
stops.campa: Sixteen seasons pass in the painter's rooms. Nothing in the record suggests Welti sees what she is becoming, and nothing suggests she asks him to look. She cooks, keeps the house, walks the slopes, and works the pendulum on her own hours: a servant in one economy and a researcher in another that pays nothing and reports to nobody. The summers give her what the factory could not: unhurried daylight, and a household where a woman holding a weighted thread over paper at the kitchen table is left alone to do it.
suggested_refs: Engelberg in the interwar season, resort village and painters' retreat

stops.name: Brittnau: the poems called Leben
stops.date_confidence: the 1930 poetry collection Leben is attested by English and German Wikipedia; neither names the place of writing or publication, so the pin is her Aargau home of record rather than an attested location
stops.campa: A book of poems appears under her name, titled Leben, life. It draws no reviews worth quoting and reaches no audience anyone recorded. She is thirty-eight, employed as a housekeeper, unknown outside two villages, and she has committed her sense of an inner order to a printed page eight years before she draws the first grid. Two further books will follow in 1953. Neither the poems nor the drawings ever argue for the order they assert. She sets it down on paper and leaves it standing there for whoever comes.
suggested_refs: Emma Kunz, Leben (1930), her first published book

stops.name: Brittnau: the pendulum turned on the ground
stops.date_confidence: the 1933 start of her earth-current investigations is attested by German Wikipedia, which gives no location; the pin to her Aargau home is reconstruction and any siting of this work at Engelberg is equally unattested
stops.campa: She turns the pendulum on the ground itself and begins investigating what she calls the currents of the earth, lines of force she holds to run beneath the visible landscape as they run beneath the visible body. This is radiesthesia at full ambition, a claim to instrumented perception rather than to fortune telling, one method answering for the sick body and for the ground under it. Five years before the first drawing, she is treating the earth as a patient, walking out with a weighted thread and a question.
suggested_refs: Radiesthesia and earth-current dowsing in interwar Switzerland

stops.name: Engelberg: the first large sheets of millimeter paper
stops.date_confidence: 1938 and the method are attested by German Wikipedia and the Serpentine Galleries; the location is not. No source places the first graph-paper works, and Engelberg is inference from the Welti arrangement running to 1939. She is forty-five turning forty-six, not forty, as some accounts have it
stops.campa: In her forty-sixth year she takes a sheet of millimetre paper, holds the pendulum above it, and marks where it points. The sheets are large and the geometry is exact. The method is repeatable: put the question, then follow where the thread goes. She calls the results research and refuses the word art. She signs nothing, dates nothing, titles almost nothing. Some sheets take a single sitting; others hold her at the table past a full day and night, the pencil following an instrument she does not claim to be directing.
stops.quote: Design and shape as dimension, rhythm, symbol and transformation of numbers and concepts.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz on her artistic energy fields, Emma Kunz Zentrum website biography page, the site's own English rendering
suggested_refs: The large-format millimetre-paper drawings begun in 1938, unsigned and undated
sources: Serpentine Galleries, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings

stops.name: Brittnau: the return, and the method hardens
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia has her resident at Brittnau from 1940 to 1947
stops.campa: She comes back to Brittnau, the village of her birth and of the two graves, and stays seven years. Here the drawing practice hardens into a discipline with a daily shape, and patients begin to find the address. From this house she will set out in 1942 for a quarry forty-five kilometres to the northeast that nobody else has any reason to visit. The village that gave her a birth certificate and two graves is now the working base for research no institution asked for and none will pay for.
suggested_refs: Kunz's Brittnau residence, 1940-1947

stops.name: Brittnau: the patients who come to the door
stops.date_confidence: the healing and diagnostic practice is attested by the Serpentine Galleries and the Emma Kunz Zentrum from the late 1930s onward; the month and year here are a placement, not an attested start date
stops.campa: They come with what conventional medicine has not resolved. She asks the pendulum over the body, or over a sheet drawn in the patient's name, what the trouble is and what will answer it. She refuses the word miracle, and she refuses to hold the capacity as exclusive: it is latent in everyone, she says, and she has only trained her own. No source records a clinic, a license, or a fee schedule. She is a healer working out of a farmhouse, which in the Swiss countryside of 1940 is an ordinary thing to be.
suggested_refs: Anton C. Meier, Emma Kunz 1892-1963: Forscherin, Naturheilpraktikerin, Kunstlerin (1994)
sources: Serpentine Galleries, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings

stops.name: Brittnau: a day and a night at a single sheet
stops.date_confidence: the sustained sessions extending beyond twenty-four hours are attested by the Serpentine Galleries without dates; the year here places the practice inside the Brittnau period
stops.campa: One sheet can hold her at the table longer than a day. She works graphite and coloured pencil across the millimetre grid without stopping to sleep, the pendulum swinging, the figure closing on itself point by point. The geometry that results is exact enough to look designed, and by her own account it is not designed at all: she is transcribing rather than composing. She never explains the mechanism, and no source records anyone at that table asking her to explain it.
stops.quote: Everything happens according to a certain regularity which I sense inside me and which never lets me rest.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz, quoted in the Serpentine Galleries exhibition text for Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings (2019)
suggested_refs: Graphite and coloured pencil on millimetre paper, the working materials of the sessions
sources: Serpentine Galleries, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings

stops.name: Brittnau: the marigolds with many heads
stops.date_confidence: undated; the marigold experiment and its photographs are attested by the Serpentine Galleries, but no source consulted assigns it a year. The date shown is a placement inside the Brittnau period and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: In the garden she turns the pendulum on marigolds, polarising them, as she puts it, and the plants come up carrying multiple flower heads on single stems. She photographs the results and keeps the photographs. It is the same claim as the drawings and the same claim as the earth currents, tested this time on something that grows and can be counted: that a weighted thread held with attention alters what it is held over. No laboratory examines the flowers and no agronomist is invited to look at them. The evidence stays in her own drawer, where it still is.
suggested_refs: Kunz's photographs of the polarised marigolds, held by the Emma Kunz Zentrum
sources: Serpentine Galleries, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings

segments.name: AION A: the Roman Quarry at Wurenlos

stops.name: Wurenlos: the boy the stone is said to have healed
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: German Wikipedia and the Emma Kunz Zentrum date Meier's healing to 1941, while the same body of sources dates Kunz's identification and naming of the stone to 1942. No source reconciles the order of the two events
stops.campa: At Wurenlos a quarry owner's son, Anton C. Meier, is left with the aftereffects of childhood polio, and the account preserved by his own foundation says the stone from the family pit is what heals him. The year given for that healing is 1941. The year given for Kunz identifying the stone's properties is 1942. The sources set the two down side by side and never explain the sequence. What is not in doubt is that a boy at Wurenlos comes out of it owing the rock a debt he will spend an adult lifetime repaying.
suggested_refs: Anton C. Meier and the Meier family quarry at Steinbruchstrasse 5, Wurenlos

stops.name: Wurenlos: the rock in the Roman quarry
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1942 by English Wikipedia and the Emma Kunz Zentrum; no month given. The mineralogical description as dolomite marl is later characterisation, not her language
stops.campa: At a quarry near Wurenlos, cut since Roman times, she tests the rock with the pendulum as she tests everything else, and one deposit answers differently from the rest. She names it AION A. It is a dolomite marl with a distinctive mineral profile, though that is not the vocabulary she has; what she has is a reading confirmed by repetition and a certainty that arrives whole. She will spend the remaining twenty-one years of her life having this stone dug out, ground down, and carried to the sick.
stops.quote: I haver never felt such powerful healing forces! This is the rock we must grind to make the powder.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz at the Wurenlos quarry, Emma Kunz Zentrum website AION A page, English site translation, transcribed verbatim including the site's apparent typo
suggested_refs: The Roman-era quarry at Wurenlos, source of AION A

stops.name: Wurenlos: the powder and the paste
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Emma Kunz Zentrum describes the extraction, grinding, and distribution across the 1940s and 1950s without fixing dates. Present-day sale in Swiss pharmacies is attested by the Serpentine Galleries and English Wikipedia, though the specific indications sometimes quoted for it are not
stops.campa: Through the forties and into the fifties the pit is worked to her instruction. AION A comes out, is ground to powder, made up as paste, given to patients and increasingly sold. She treats it as a discovery of the same rank as the drawings, a second research field with a single subject: what the body lacks and how the earth supplies it. The rock outlives her by generations. It is still cut at the same face and still sold across Swiss counters, under the name she gave it at the pit.
stops.quote: The universal power of AION A must be made accessible to mankind.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz, Emma Kunz Zentrum website AION A page, English site translation
suggested_refs: AION A powder as sold in Swiss pharmacies, quarried at the original site
sources: Serpentine Galleries, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings

stops.name: Wurenlos: the grotto in the hillside
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Emma Kunz Zentrum records her repeated returns to the grotto and both quoted phrases without attaching years to them
stops.campa: She goes back to the quarry again and again, not only for the stone but for the place. The cutting has opened a grotto in the hillside and she sits inside it. Her own account of why is domestic and exact: she comes to recharge, body and soul, the way a battery is recharged. She calls it a place of strength and says aloud that she would like it one day to be a meeting ground where healing and culture are held together. Twenty-three years after her death someone will do precisely that with the hill.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz on her returns to the Wurenlos grotto, quoted in the Emma Kunz Zentrum website biography page; a phrase quoted in situ rather than a full sentence
suggested_refs: The grotto cut into the Wurenlos quarry face, later the centre of the Emma Kunz Zentrum

stops.name: Waldstatt: the move under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951 by German Wikipedia; no month given
stops.campa: At fifty-nine she leaves the Aargau for Waldstatt, a village of a few hundred in Appenzell Ausserrhoden under the limestone wall of the Santis. She holds the place to be spiritually significant and says so plainly. It is steep pasture under exposed rock, with weather that arrives without warning, two cantons east of the valley of looms she was born in. She will spend twelve years here, drawing, receiving patients, and directing the Wurenlos quarry from a hundred kilometres off.
suggested_refs: Waldstatt, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, below the Santis massif

stops.name: Waldstatt: the consulting room
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Waldstatt healing practice is attested by the Emma Kunz Zentrum and by Meier's 1994 biography as cited through English Wikipedia, without a start date
stops.campa: The village learns what she is inside a season. Patients come up from the valley and down from the farms with complaints that have already been to a doctor. She works as she has worked since Brittnau: the pendulum first, the sheet if a sheet is called for, the powder from Wurenlos if the powder is called for. Appenzell has a long tolerance for naturopaths and she does not have to argue for her existence here. The village knows her as a healer. Asked what she is, she answers that she is a researcher.
suggested_refs: Anton C. Meier's 1994 biography of Kunz as researcher, naturopath, and artist

stops.name: Waldstatt: Neuartige Zeichnungsmethode
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953 by German and English Wikipedia; no month given
stops.campa: She self-publishes Neuartige Zeichnungsmethode, a new method of drawing, setting out in print what she has done since 1938: the pendulum over the grid, the graph paper as instrument rather than decoration. It is the closest she comes to explaining herself to a stranger, and even here she frames the work as method and research rather than as something made to be looked at. From a village of a few hundred she tells Switzerland how drawing can measure what cannot otherwise be seen. Switzerland does not reply.
stops.quote: Shape and form expressed as measurement, rhythm, symbol and transformation of figure and principle.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz on her creative work, Emma Kunz Zentrum website biography page, the site's own English rendering; the original German is not given there
suggested_refs: Emma Kunz, Neuartige Zeichnungsmethode (self-published, 1953)

stops.name: Waldstatt: the second book of the same year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953 by English Wikipedia, which gives the title in English as The Miracle of Creative Revelation; the month is a placement to keep the two 1953 books in order and is not attested
stops.campa: A companion volume follows in the same year, known to English readers as The Miracle of Creative Revelation. Neither book sells, neither is reviewed in a journal that survives to be cited, neither is translated while she lives. She prints them at her own cost in a country whose art world does not know her name and whose medical establishment would not have her. These two volumes are the whole of her explanation. Everything else she leaves behind is graph paper carrying no signature and no date.
suggested_refs: Emma Kunz, Das Wunder schopfender Offenbarung (self-published, 1953)

stops.name: Waldstatt: the work addressed to a later century
stops.date_confidence: the attested statement is the one quoted here, from the Emma Kunz Zentrum; the widely repeated claim that she predicted her work would be understood in five hundred years is not traceable to any Kunz statement in the sources consulted and is flagged as tradition. The year is a placement in her last decade
stops.campa: She tells those close to her that the work is not for her own time. Accounts of what exactly she said differ, and the number most often repeated in her name, five hundred years, traces to a French admirer writing after her death rather than to her own mouth. What she is recorded saying is narrower and stranger: the drawings are made for the century after hers. She seeks no exhibition and courts no dealer. The sheets stay stacked where they were made, in a village that has no gallery and wants none.
stops.quote: My drawings are designed for the 21st century. They also convey composition and form as dimension, rhythm, symbol and transformation of numbers and principles.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz, quoted on the Emma Kunz Zentrum website Museum page, English site translation
suggested_refs: The stacked, unexhibited drawings as Kunz left them at Waldstatt

stops.name: Waldstatt: the sixteenth of January
stops.date_confidence: attested; death date and place agree across English and German Wikipedia and the Emma Kunz Zentrum. The size of the surviving body of work does not agree: English Wikipedia says four hundred drawings, the Emma Kunz Zentrum says around six hundred, and no source reconciles them
stops.campa: She dies at Waldstatt on the sixteenth of January, seventy years old. Behind her are the sheets: four hundred of them by the count her English record gives, six hundred by the count her own foundation keeps, and the two numbers have never been brought into agreement. Almost nobody outside her circle has seen any of them. They go into storage rather than into a gallery, a body of research finished and closed, addressed to readers she has already said will belong to the century after hers.
suggested_refs: The surviving corpus of Kunz drawings, counted at four hundred or six hundred depending on the source

stops.name: Waldstatt: the grave no source names
stops.date_confidence: the burial itself is unrecorded: no location, marker, or date appears in English or German Wikipedia, the Emma Kunz Zentrum institutional history, or the Serpentine Galleries material. The date shown is a placement days after the attested death and asserts nothing
stops.campa: She is buried, and no source consulted records where. Not the English record, not the German, not her own foundation's history, not the material published by the London gallery that will make her famous in Britain. The woman who spent a life insisting hidden things can be located leaves her own grave unlocated in the literature. The visitors, when they finally come, go instead to a quarry a hundred kilometres west of Waldstatt, where her stone is still being cut out of the hill she chose.
suggested_refs: Waldstatt parish burial registers, not consulted in this research pass
sources: gap: no burial location in English or German Wikipedia, emma-kunz.com, or Serpentine Galleries materials

stops.name: Aarau: Der Fall Emma Kunz
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1973 at the Aargauer Kunsthaus by German Wikipedia and the Emma Kunz Zentrum, with Heiny Widmer as curator; no month established. The German title is Der Fall Emma Kunz, which English Wikipedia renders as Der Fall von Emma Kunz. No source gives the number of sheets hung
stops.campa: Ten years after her death the drawings are shown in public for the first time, at the Aargauer Kunsthaus, brought forward by the curator Heiny Widmer under the title Der Fall Emma Kunz, the case of Emma Kunz. The rooms fill with unsigned, undated geometry that no category in the building accounts for. It is the moment the researcher becomes, against her own framing and without her consent, an artist. Harald Szeemann reaches the work in the same decade and begins telling Europe what he thinks it is.
stops.quote: Her gift was an awareness of connections that contradicted both normal experience and scientific interpretations of the laws of Nature and art. This was a supernatural event, a miracle that, in revealing divine truths conveyed a secret impulse on a par with that of cosmic creation. Emma Kunz's drawings are attempts to find a universal connection. They are the records of her concentration on the question of the Whole.
stops.quote_source: Harald Szeemann, quoted in the Serpentine Galleries exhibition text for Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings (2019); original publication and date not given there
suggested_refs: Der Fall Emma Kunz, Aargauer Kunsthaus, 1973, curated by Heiny Widmer

stops.name: Dusseldorf: the sheets leave Switzerland
stops.date_confidence: undated; German Wikipedia names Dusseldorf and Paris as later exhibition cities without venue, curator, or year. The date shown is a placeholder inside the post-1973 wave and asserts nothing. The city pin is a centroid, not a venue
stops.campa: The sheets travel out of Switzerland. Dusseldorf stands in the record of her posthumous exhibitions with no gallery attached, no curator, and no year; what it marks is a direction rather than an event. Within a generation of her death the drawings have moved from a village archive in Appenzell into the museum circuit of German-speaking Europe, carried there by people who never met her and who describe the work in a vocabulary she declined to use about it while she was alive to be asked.
suggested_refs: The unidentified Dusseldorf showing named in German Wikipedia's exhibition list

stops.name: Paris: the five hundred years
stops.date_confidence: undated; German Wikipedia names Paris as an exhibition city without venue or year, and the Emma Kunz Zentrum quotes Larcher without dating the remark. The date shown is a placeholder and the pin is a city centroid
stops.campa: Paris is named the same way, a city on a list with no venue and no year against it. What survives from Paris with a name attached is a sentence: Professor H. Larcher, considering the work she left, says that people such as Emma Kunz come at best once in five hundred years. The number is his, offered after her death, not hers about herself. It attaches to her anyway, and a good deal of what gets written about her afterward repeats the figure as a prophecy she is supposed to have made.
stops.quote: People such as Emma Kunz live at best once every 500 years, and even then we do not always have the good fortune to receive such a witness as that delivered in her bequeathed work.
stops.quote_source: Prof. H. Larcher, Paris, quoted on the Emma Kunz Zentrum website biography page
suggested_refs: The Larcher remark as the traceable origin of the five-hundred-year legend

stops.name: Wurenlos: the centre founded at the quarry
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1986 by the Emma Kunz Zentrum and English Wikipedia; no month given
stops.campa: Anton C. Meier, the man the stone is said to have healed in 1941, founds a centre at the Wurenlos quarry: the grotto in the cut rock, the working pit, her drawings, her papers, and the AION A trade all held under one institution at Steinbruchstrasse 5. What she ran alone, a healer digging in a hillside with nothing behind her, now has an address, a legal form, and a successor. The wish she spoke aloud in the grotto is granted twenty-three years after she stops being there to ask for it.
stops.quote_source: Emma Kunz's stated wish, quoted within the Emma Kunz Zentrum website biography page; a phrase quoted in situ rather than a full sentence
suggested_refs: The Emma Kunz Zentrum, Steinbruchstrasse 5, CH-5436 Wurenlos

stops.name: Wurenlos: the museum opens
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia gives 17 October 1991 for the opening, English Wikipedia gives the year and the figure of roughly seventy major works shown
stops.campa: The museum opens on the seventeenth of October at the quarry, showing some seventy of her major sheets. Visitors who come for the geometry walk past the pit where the stone is still cut, and visitors who come for the stone walk past the drawings. The two halves of the work share one address because for her they were never two projects. The museum stands directly on the working pit, in the arrangement she described aloud in the grotto and did not live to see built.
suggested_refs: The Emma Kunz Museum at the Wurenlos quarry, opened 17 October 1991

stops.name: Zurich: Richtkrafte fur das 21. Jahrhundert
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia gives the Kunsthaus Zurich exhibition Richtkrafte fur das 21. Jahrhundert, 21 May to 1 August 1999, with Rudolf Steiner, Joseph Beuys, and Andrej Belyj
stops.campa: The Kunsthaus Zurich hangs her sheets in Richtkrafte fur das 21. Jahrhundert, guiding forces for the twenty-first century, from May into August, beside Rudolf Steiner's blackboard drawings and work by Joseph Beuys and Andrej Belyj. It is the first large frame that takes her literally, a show organised around the century she addressed the drawings to, mounted in the year before that century opens. Zurich lies an hour from the quarry and did not look at her once while she was alive to be looked at.
suggested_refs: Richtkrafte fur das 21. Jahrhundert, Kunsthaus Zurich, 21 May to 1 August 1999

stops.name: Santa Monica: 3 x Abstraction
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2005 by English Wikipedia; no month established. The venue is the Santa Monica Museum of Art at its Bergamot Station address, where it stood from 1998, not the Ocean Park location some coordinate sets give
stops.campa: At Bergamot Station the Santa Monica Museum of Art shows 3 x Abstraction, Catherine de Zegher's pairing of Kunz with Hilma af Klint and Agnes Martin. The exhibition and its book fix her permanently beside af Klint: two women who made large geometric abstractions by a method they refused to call invention, who insisted the result was research rather than art, and who each addressed the work to a public they knew would arrive after them. Paper worked with a pendulum in the Wiggertal hangs on a Californian coast.
suggested_refs: Catherine de Zegher, 3 x Abstraction: New Methods of Drawing by Hilma af Klint, Emma Kunz, and Agnes Martin (Yale University Press, 2005)

stops.name: Venice: The Encyclopedic Palace
stops.date_confidence: attested; English Wikipedia's exhibition list names the 55th Venice Biennale, The Encyclopedic Palace, Central Pavilion, which is the 2013 edition in the Giardini. The June date is the Biennale's opening month, not a documented hanging date
stops.campa: Massimiliano Gioni builds the fifty-fifth Biennale around the Encyclopedic Palace, cosmologies and diagrams made largely by people outside the profession of art, and Kunz's sheets hang in the Central Pavilion in the Giardini. She is placed among visionaries, autodidacts, and the institutionally unclassifiable, which is accurate, and among artists, which she spent a lifetime declining. Forty years after Aarau the sheets hang in the Giardini under labels written entirely by other people.
suggested_refs: The Encyclopedic Palace, 55th Venice Biennale, Central Pavilion, Giardini, 2013

stops.name: Munich: Weltempfanger at the Lenbachhaus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2018/2019 by German Wikipedia, which names Weltempfanger at the Stadtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau Munchen with Georgiana Houghton and Hilma af Klint; the month shown is a placement inside the run
stops.campa: The Lenbachhaus mounts Weltempfanger, world receiver, and hangs Kunz with Georgiana Houghton and Hilma af Klint: three women who each made abstraction before or beside the recognised avant-garde and each attributed the method to something other than personal invention. The show runs from 2018 into 2019, and it puts Kunz in the company of Houghton's spirit drawings and af Klint's temple paintings, which she never had while she was working. Munich reads across the three of them a lineage that no art history written in Kunz's lifetime had a name for or a shelf to put it on.

stops.name: London: Emma Kunz, Visionary Drawings
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Serpentine Galleries give 23 March to 19 May 2019 for her first United Kingdom solo exhibition, with over forty drawings and benches quarried from AION A
stops.campa: The Serpentine gives her a first British solo show, Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings, from the twenty-third of March to the nineteenth of May, over forty sheets that almost nobody outside Switzerland has seen. Christodoulos Panayiotou conceives the installation and has benches cut from AION A, quarried at Wurenlos, set into the gallery. Londoners sit on her stone to look at her paper. The wall texts call her a researcher, which is the word she used, and an artist, which is the word she refused.
suggested_refs: Emma Kunz: Visionary Drawings, Serpentine South Gallery, 23 March to 19 May 2019

stops.name: Aarau: Emma Kunz Cosmos
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2021 at the Aargauer Kunsthaus by its own exhibition page and English Wikipedia; the month is not established here, and the figures of roughly sixty drawings and fourteen contemporary artists come from the museum's own material
stops.campa: The Aargauer Kunsthaus returns to her forty-eight years after the first showing, with Emma Kunz Cosmos: some sixty drawings, many of them exhibited for the first time, set among fourteen living artists invited to work in her vicinity. The building that first admitted her is still arguing the case it opened in 1973, and still hanging sheets she called research in rooms built for art. Fifty-eight years after her death, what exactly the case of Emma Kunz is has not been settled by the people who keep putting it up on their walls.
suggested_refs: Emma Kunz Cosmos, Aargauer Kunsthaus, Aarau, 2021

stops.name: Wurenlos: the quarry made a protected place
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2021 by German Wikipedia, which records an Aargau heritage-protection award to the Emma Kunz Foundation for the Wurenlos site; the month shown is a placement
stops.campa: The canton of Aargau gives the Emma Kunz Foundation a heritage-protection award for the Wurenlos site: the Roman pit, the grotto, the museum above it. The rock is still cut and still sold across Swiss counters as a wellness product. The drawings hang in the building on the hill. A working quarry when she found it in 1942 is now a monument under cantonal protection, to a woman who walked in with a weighted thread and told the owner which rock to grind.
suggested_refs: The Aargau heritage-protection award to the Emma Kunz Foundation, 2021
